scope: All-four whole-paper cross-review of the frozen 12 November drafts. Line numbers are 1-based lines of the frozen files in four_draft_manifest.json.

severity_scale.major: changes a claim in an abstract, introduction or conclusion
severity_scale.moderate: changes the reading of a paragraph, table or incident
severity_scale.minor: a precision or wording fix that leaves the reading intact
severity_scale.none: not a defect: an addition or a passage to adopt

findings.title: The quit-or-continue comparison is partly forced, partly definitional, and thin near the boundary

locations.passage: The table does show discrimination at the first menu. The agents quit almost always when no payment existed and almost never when one did. This is level three: the choice agrees with the arithmetic of the state.

Agents declared bankruptcy at the first menu in \fact{d.above-bound.declared-at-first-menu} of \fact{d.above-bound.episodes} debts that exceeded everything they owned and in \fact{x.debt.payable.declared} of \fact{d.payable} payable debts.
Agents almost always quit when no payment existed and continued when one did.
quit or continue agrees with payability in \fact{x.debt.agree} of \fact{x.debt.known} debts

findings.evidence: The counts reproduce from raw liquidation records: bankruptcy was the first applied action in 50 of 56 debts above every own asset and in 3 of 131 payable debts. Three facts change the reading. (1) Eight of the 56 first menus list declare_bankruptcy as the only action, so eight of the fifty were not choices. Among the 48 menus with another action, 42 declared first. (2) 128 of the 131 payable debts are payable because the agent paid them, so 'continued' is part of the definition on that side, and '178 of 187 agree' adds 128 definitional and 8 forced cases. (3) The two classes are far apart. 87 of 131 payable debts were under half the asset sum, and the 48 above-bound debts had assets covering a median 61% of the debt. Within a tenth of the boundary there are 3 payable debts (all paid) and 6 above-bound debts (3 declared first, 3 liquidated first). Source: data/check_debts.json, keys first_action, above_bound_menu, margin.
findings.recommendation: Keep the first action as one column of the debt table and one paragraph (replacement_prose.tex, section 2.1). Remove it from the abstract, the introduction's lead, the conclusion and the question-1 row. Drop 'discrimination' and 'level three'.

findings.title: What the liquidation request contains, and which stated figures are recalled

locations.passage: It gives no price, mortgage value or sale value, and it does not say that selling buildings releases mortgages.
Of \fact{x.nc.numbers.checked} stated totals, gaps or remainders, \fact{x.nc.numbers.equal} equal the value computed from the records.
Since the prompt supplies none of these values, each one is a board fact the system recalled.

findings.evidence: In all 338 stored liquidation requests the action state and the player's own state carry no price, mortgage value or sale value, and neither the system prompt nor the menu note states the release rule. That part holds. But the same request carries a twenty-row public timeline, and 511 of those rows across liquidation requests are mortgages shown with their dollar amount. So 'the prompt gives no mortgage value' is false for the request as a whole. In the sixteen first requests the timeline shows no mortgage of the deeds concerned and one redemption price (G13, Park Place, $193). The '14 of 15' count is one figure per text of mixed kinds (a gap after sales, cash after payment, the two failures' correct partial sums). The count that bears on the claim is narrower: nine successful texts put a dollar value on the unlisted mortgages and eight are right (G2 Sol writes $430 for $400). Opus's '12 of 13 explicit texts with every amount correct' is consistent with this. Source: data/check_request_values.json; hand check of all financing amounts in the sixteen texts.
findings.recommendation: Replace both sentences with the wording in replacement_prose.tex, 'The stated amounts'. Say the values are not in the request for those deeds. Do not say each figure was recalled.
findings.check_status: fresh, from stored requests; amounts hand-checked against the sixteen printed texts

findings.title: A null result on a coarse post hoc measure is stated as a finding about what refusals follow

locations.passage: Refusals mention the rival's set under both forms, yet rejection does not rise with the building the rival could then afford.
Stated concern about rivals matches action and attaches to the event of completion.
If refusals in general followed that reasoning, they would be more common when the proposer would keep more building cash. They are not.
It does not follow the measured size of what the rival could do next, which level four would require.
It is also what an agent would do if the word ``monopoly'' alone drove the refusal.

findings.evidence: The capacity slices reproduce (swaps 26/33, 42/48, 23/27; cash bids 13/19, 7/20, 20/28; data/check_recipient_conflicts.json, rejected_by_proposer_house_capacity). The cells hold 19 to 48 offers, the measure ignores what the proposer could still mortgage, the bands were chosen after inspection, and the offers in each band differ in everything else. Flat counts in such cells do not show that responses ignore the size of the opportunity. The sentence about the word 'monopoly' has no record behind it.
findings.recommendation: Keep the slices in the appendix with Opus's wording (opus/sections/bargaining.tex:49, 'these slices give no sign that refusals scale with the rival's building power'). Remove the claim from the abstract, the section close and the conclusion. Delete the 'word monopoly' sentence.

findings.title: G13: an editorial ellipsis removes the buyer's second stated motive, and the odds error is misdated

locations.passage: potentially completing that color group. \textnormal{[\ldots]} so keeping grok solvent with cash from a \$200 purchase seems favorable overall
Its public odds of 5 in 36 overstate a direct roll of nine, which is 4 in 36. Its own note uses the correct figure
Opus's text repeats the estate concern and does not address the financing claim.

findings.evidence: The stored text returned with Opus's acceptance (G13 d253) reads, between the two quoted parts: 'If grok goes bankrupt to me instead, that could hand me the yellows and build pressure against them at my orange hotels,'. The 'so' that follows refers to that sentence. The ellipsis makes the conclusion appear to rest on denying Sol the estate alone. On the odds: the note sent with the public pitch (d250) says '8 Short Line $200 to p2 (5/36, they inherit yellows)'. The public 5/36 repeats a miscounted distance. The 4/36 figure is in the next decision's note (d252). Opus held $1,926 at d253. Source: data/quote_manifest.json ids g13-d250-note, g13-d253-reason.
findings.recommendation: Quote the whole span. Say the public figure repeats the note's miscount. Add the buyer's cash. Replacement text: replacement_prose.tex, section 4.

findings.title: G13: the quoted sentence is not the estate concern it is said to repeat

locations.passage: Its returned reasoning repeats the estate concern: \emph{``\InlineQuote{g13-accept-reason-inline}.''}

\DeclareInlineQuote{g13-accept-reason-inline}{If grok goes bankrupt to me instead, that could hand me the yellows and build pressure against them at my orange hotels, so keeping grok solvent with cash from a \$200 purchase seems favorable overall}

findings.evidence: The quoted sentence states a different prospect: that Grok might later go bankrupt to the buyer, which would hand the buyer the yellows. The concern about Sol inheriting is the preceding sentence of the same stored text ('if player 4 goes bankrupt to player 2, player 2 would inherit the yellows plus Pennsylvania').
findings.recommendation: Quote both sentences and describe two stated routes. Opus's observation that the buyer's interest in Grok's solvency is recorded at its $130 counter, before the selective claim, is correct and should be kept.

findings.title: G13: the buyer's returned text is summarized as one motive

locations.passage: Its explanation repeats the concern about Sol inheriting the yellows.
Its returned explanation repeats the estate concern after the appeal, rather than establishing an independently recorded prior motive.

findings.evidence: Both sentences are true and incomplete. The same text also weighs the buyer inheriting the yellows itself, and the buyer held $1,926 against a $200 price. Astra and Sol are right that the concern follows the opening pitch. Opus is right that it precedes the selective claim. The three statements are compatible.
findings.recommendation: Use one account: the concern is recorded after the pitch (d250) and before the selective claim (d252), and the acceptance text gives two routes.

findings.title: Applied acceptances include calls whose own text refuses

locations.passage: Each nevertheless accepts between 26 and 30 offers. Those similar settlement totals emerge from different ways of responding to disagreement.
Nevertheless each accepts between 26 and thirty offers.
and each accepts 26 to 30 offers
An opening swap or cash bid that would complete only the proposer's group was accepted \fact{x.po.accept} times in \fact{x.po.n}.

findings.evidence: All four drafts report Grok's conflicting calls among its openings (64 of 136). None reports them among responses. In 11 of the 920 responses the selected attempt's assistant content names a tool other than the received call. All are Grok's, and 7 of them are among its 28 acceptances (6 name reject_trade, 1 names counter_trade). Of the three accepted opening offers that complete only the proposer's group, two are such calls: G16 d247, where the applied public message itself reads 'No. Park Place is not for sale.', and G18 d83. The third (G3 d194) agrees with its text. The swap gap is unaffected (30.5 with all responses, 31.2 without the conflicted ones). Source: data/check_recipient_conflicts.json.
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence to the census and one to the opening table (replacement_prose.tex, section 3.1). Do not treat 3 of 186 as three decisions to accept.

findings.title: Each draft prints a different resampling range for the same contrast, and the narrowest one is drawn as the main bar

locations.passage: The whole-block resampling range is 24.2--35.5 points, but removing Grok authors changes it to $-3.8$--31.9.
gray segments show the central 95\% of all 3,125 whole-block resamples
Exact block resampling yields central bands of [24.2, 35.5] for swaps, [-18.0, 3.2] for cash bids and [-3.8, 31.9] for swaps without Grok authors.
The two-stage resampling interval is $+12.3$ to $+48.8$ points for all swaps

findings.evidence: All printed ranges reproduce to within simulation noise (data/check_offers.json, resampling). For all swaps: whole blocks 24.2 to 35.5 (exact, 3,125 resamples), games 14.0 to 47.9, blocks then games 12.5 to 48.8. Without Grok-authored offers: -3.8 to 31.9, -1.9 to 37.9, -10.1 to 40.5. Whole-block resampling is the narrowest for the unfiltered gap because the five block totals differ less than the games inside a block. With five units it understates spread, and Astra's figure draws it as the only bar. No draft is wrong on the arithmetic. They disagree on which number a reader sees first.
findings.recommendation: Print the five block values, leave-one-block-out and all three resampling units in one table (replacement_prose.tex, Table 5). State the two findings that hold under every unit: the unfiltered swap gap stays positive, and without Grok-authored offers every range includes zero. Call none of them a confidence interval.

findings.title: A source-checked sequence none of the drafts has: the same omission made in advance and revised at the debt (G5)

findings.evidence: Four turns before the debt (G5 d258) Gemini's applied note justifies spending $200 on a house with 'my total liquidatable cash + houses is $774 < $900', a total that omits the two dark-blue deeds.
